title: Police shooting victim had expressed hope for the future
subtitle: David Doucette had moved into a boarding house in October and was turning his life around before an altercation with police that left him dead.
article: The man shot and killed by police on Feb. 18 outside a Spadina Rd. boarding house had told others he had "no family and no friends," but expressed hope for the future.

David Doucette, 49, was a client of St. Michael's Hospital's CATCH program for people who are homeless, have addictions or suffer mental illness - or some combination of the three - but had recently turned his life around.
He moved into a seven-room boarding house for men in October 2014, and shortly afterward told a social worker that "he was the happiest he's been in his entire life."
"He started writing a book on his journey. He shared that through the writing, he is experiencing some emotions that he hasn't felt in years," said the worker, who asked not to be identified.
"He said he has always wondered about his purpose in life and he's found it: to write," the worker noted in a meeting with Doucette last December.
Another man in his 60s was taken to hospital with stab wounds to the neck. The second victim, also a resident of the boarding house, has not been identified and is still recovering in hospital.

The house, run by Homes First, accepts high-functioning men referred by hospitals, shelters and addiction treatment agencies. Because the house has no full-time staff, residents must be relatively independent and not need a lot of support, said Homes First executive director Patricia Mueller.
"Some of our other houses have police called every day. I can't remember the last time police were called to that house," Mueller said.

A short man with a slender build, Doucette was always clean-shaven and kept his dark blond hair cropped neatly, the agency worker said. A carpenter by trade, he had lived in both Nova Scotia and Ontario, though by the time he arrived at the boarding house, he was not working anymore.
"He was very quiet, well-read and enjoyed writing poetry," said the case worker, who met with him twice a week.
Doucette had recently spoken about enjoying reading Nietzsche and purchased books of philosophy whenever he could, reading them alone in his room.

"Around Christmas time, he told our staff member that he didn't really celebrate it because he had no family or friends," said Mueller. "Our staff had said, 'Well, here are all the places you can go to drop in,' and he said, 'No, I don't think so. I'll probably stay home.'"
The case worker was shocked by the deadly altercation, saying Doucette had been getting along well with the other residents.
"My last memory of him is he being happy about embracing life and moving forward, just accepting himself as a person. I remember him saying, 'You know, I'm just happy to be me.'"
